q: Are delivery riders' own two-wheelers part of my Scope 3, and in which category?
title: Gig riders' two-wheelers: which scope?
short: Yes. Riders' own two-wheelers are not your Scope 1 because you neither own nor control them. Deliveries you pay riders for are a purchased transport service, so they go in Scope 3 Category 4. Deliveries a customer pays for separately belong in Category 9. Estimate from trips, distance and a per-km factor.
audience: Delivery platforms, e-commerce sellers and restaurants using gig riders

p: Scope 1 covers vehicles you own or control. A rider who owns the scooter, buys the petrol and is paid per delivery is a supplier of transport services, even if your app assigns the orders. Company-owned or leased bikes that you fuel would be Scope 1.

ul: You pay the rider or the delivery partner for outbound delivery of your sold goods: Category 4, upstream transportation and distribution, which includes outbound transport the company pays for.
The customer pays a delivery platform directly and you do not buy the service: Category 9 for you as the seller, which is downstream transport.
A delivery platform buying rides from riders to fulfil its own service: Category 4 for the platform.
Riders delivering to you, such as inbound parcels paid by you: also Category 4.

ol: Take the number of deliveries and the average distance per delivery, including the pickup leg, from app or GPS logs.
Total km x a per-km factor for the vehicle type. For a petrol two-wheeler, the factor is 2.31 kg CO2 per litre divided by km per litre.
For electric two-wheelers, use kWh per km x 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh.
Count only trips made for you. A rider working for several platforms is shared.

example.title: Worked example: one month of outbound deliveries
lines: Deliveries: 30,000; average 7 km each including pickup leg (from app logs)
Petrol at 45 km per litre (assumed fleet average): 2,10,000 / 45 = 4,666.7 litres
CO2: 4,666.7 x 2.31 = 10,780 kg, about 10.8 t for the month in Category 4
example.note: Survey a sample of riders for mileage and the petrol versus electric split; record it as an assumption.

senseible: Senseible keeps transport invoices in the Scope 3 supplier evidence trail and, where only payout spend is known, provides a spend-based estimate labelled as spend-based with wider uncertainty. A trip-and-distance estimate like the one above is firmer and stays your own calculation.
